newsitem.title: SPAIN: Far East and Latam lead ex-Madrid air cargo boom.
newsitem.headline: Far East and Latam lead ex-Madrid air cargo boom.

text.p: Demand for air cargo space ex-Madrid has soared this month, particularly on routes to Latin America and the Far East as the peak export season starts, airlines and general sales agents said.
Average indicated rates across the Atlantic are higher than in September because the cheapest offers from integrators have dropped out of the market, not because airlines have raised their rates.
There was margin for prices to rise on some routes, but they were unlikely to do so, industry sources said.
"There's very strong demand to the Far East, for cargoes like furs, pharmaceutical products and spare parts," said a GSA with a mixture of European and Oriental clients.
"Flights are full to capacity," said an airline cargo salesman. "There's a lot of demand in every direction."
Lufthansa reported strong business to the Far East and also to Dubai where many of its flights make a technical stop.

There has been demand for shipping a lot of telecommunications equipment to South America recently and big loads have struggled to find space, a European carrier said. It was quoting rates as high as 480 pesetas a kilo to Chile or 440 pesetas a kilo to Sao Paolo for urgent and premium loads.
Some carriers were also quoting rates to Buenos Aires in the high 400s. Prices were cheaper with Pluna, the Uruguayan carrier, but it rarely had space, freight forwarders said.
"October, November and December are the peak months but by December capacity is limited by higher passenger demand," another GSA said of the transatlantic business.

The surge in cargo demand comes at a time when some airlines have reduced capacity or frequencies of their passenger services for the winter, which in some cases accentuates the pressure on cargo space.

One U.S. carrier has switched to a Boeing 767 instead of a 747 for its daily transatlantic flight, for example, and Iberia has replaced 747-200s with Airbus A340s on its daily Madrid-Mexico flight, although it says that in practice cargo capacity with the new aircraft could be higher.

The Spanish flag carrier was also planning to put on a second weekly 747 freighter to Buenos Aires, possibly from this week, to cope with the extra demand and can schedule extra DC-8 freighters on other Latin American routes such as Sao Paolo as necessary.
Despite the squeeze on cargo space, most airlines and sales agents said their prices were unchanged and were likely to remain steady because airlines were aware the surge in demand was short-term.
"Prices could rise - it's the only time of year they can, but it wouldn't be worth doing because we'd have to bring them down again early next year," one GSA said.
"Prices will stay the same," added the European airline official.
British Airways said its peseta prices had not changed for the winter season but added they might if sterling rose further against the peseta.
BA is increasing its cargo capacity between Madrid and London by substituting 767s for narrowbody aircraft on two flights a day Monday to Friday and one flight on Sundays from the end of this month.
The downward pressure on North Atlantic prices has eased but competition is still fierce and rates for large loads relatively low, airlines said.
"Winter shipments of footwear will help from now until January or February, but I'm not very optimistic about prices," a U.S. airline representative said of his North Atlantic business.

The average price for Madrid-New York has risen since September to around 165 pesetas a kilo for 100 kilos minimum because there are fewer cut price offers in the market. Prices for 100 kilos minimum range from 133 pesetas to 200 pesetas a kilo.

One airline said it sometimes charged as little as 110 pesetas a kilo but only for much larger loads of very dense products. The market price for pallet cargo was around 125 or 130 pesetas a kilo to New York, it said. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
